extracted.populationAffected: Owners of vehicles primarily used for app-based food delivery

scope.note: Declines the whole policy based on vehicle use. This is a decline rule.

criteria.label: Legislation, regulation and guidance
criteria.reasoning: No provision of the Insurance Act, its regulations, the UDAP Rule or FSRA guidance in the registry appears to bar a decline based on commercial delivery use of a personal vehicle. Under Take All Comers the rule still needs the regulator's approval before the insurer may use it.

evidence.quote: primarily used for food delivery through app-based platforms

criteria.label: Human Rights Code and Charter
criteria.reasoning: The delivery use of a vehicle is not a protected ground under the Human Rights Code. Nothing in the wording suggests it would act as a close proxy for one, because it applies to every applicant on the same factual basis.

criteria.label: Already exists in the market
criteria.reasoning: The framework lists part-time use of a vehicle for package delivery (FX-02) and business use (FX-01) as common decline rules, and AP-06 (Oakridge Lane Mutual, 2015) declines any automobile used for commercial purposes. DR-003 applies the same logic to app-based food delivery and limits it to vehicles "primarily" used that way, so it is no broader than the approved commercial-use rule.

criteria.label: Accurate pricing and underwriting
criteria.reasoning: Delivery work changes how much and where a vehicle is driven, which the principle names as risk factors. The rule reflects the actual use of the insured vehicle.

evidence.quote: significantly increases kilometres driven, time on the road, and frequency of stops in high-traffic areas

criteria.label: Absence of unfair discrimination, bias or proxies
criteria.reasoning: App-based delivery work is concentrated among newcomers and students, so the rule could fall unevenly on those groups. The trigger itself is vehicle use, so this is a low-level indirect effect to monitor rather than a proxy.

criteria.label: Accessible products and coverages
criteria.reasoning: Delivery drivers still need coverage, and a decline pushes them to find a commercial or delivery-specific product. Access is reasonable only if such products are available at a workable price.

evidence.quote: Decline to insure any vehicle primarily used for food delivery

criteria.label: Cost mitigation
criteria.reasoning: Keeping commercial delivery exposure out of the personal auto pool stops other policyholders from subsidising it. The rule does not add cost for consumers who drive only for personal use.

evidence.quote: beyond what personal auto rating contemplates

criteria.label: Balanced profitability and consumer interests
criteria.reasoning: The rule targets a real change in use rather than a group of people. Limiting it to primary use is a proportionate line.

criteria.label: Clear consumer communications
criteria.reasoning: Consumers who deliver a few evenings a week may not know whether they count as "primarily" using the vehicle for delivery. The insurer should explain the test and point them to suitable coverage.

criteria.label: Not subjective
criteria.reasoning: Whether use is "primary" will depend on the applicant's declaration and the underwriter's reading of it. A measurable test would remove the judgment call.

criteria.label: Not arbitrary
criteria.reasoning: The rule follows an established category of decline (commercial delivery use) rather than an invented threshold. There is no numeric cut-off that needs justifying.

criteria.label: Direct relationship to risk
criteria.reasoning: More kilometres, more time on the road and frequent stops in traffic link directly to collision exposure. The rationale states a clear, plausible mechanism.

criteria.label: Actuarial support
criteria.reasoning: The rationale explains the exposure mechanism but gives no figures. No actuarial data or analysis is attached to the submission. Because a comparable approved rule exists and this one is no stricter, the gap is unlikely to change the outcome, but the analysis should be on file before approval.

criteria.label: Definition clarity
criteria.reasoning: "Primarily used" is not defined, for example by hours or share of kilometres. Without a definition the same driver could be treated differently by different brokers.

criteria.label: Public policy filter
criteria.reasoning: No: nothing about this proposal appears inappropriate for a consumer protection regulator to approve. Separating commercial delivery from personal coverage is established practice, provided delivery drivers can buy suitable coverage.

precedents.explanation: Framework common example: part-time use of a vehicle for package delivery. DR-003 covers food delivery and applies only to primary use, which is narrower than "part-time".
Approved rule declines any automobile used for commercial purposes. App-based delivery is one kind of commercial use; DR-003 is a specific application of the same principle.

Pending Birchwood Insurance Group rule declines peer-to-peer car sharing "even occasionally". Same commercial-use logic, but DR-070 has no primary-use limit; review together so occasional versus primary use is treated consistently.
Pending Birchwood Insurance Group rule declines home-based business client visits more than 3 times a week. Another business-use rule with a different usage threshold.

consumerImpact.whoCouldBeRefused: Gig workers whose vehicle is mainly used for app-based food delivery.
consumerImpact.likelyConsequence: They would need a commercial or delivery-specific policy or endorsement. If none is available at a workable price, they may lose their income source.
vulnerableGroups: Newcomers and students doing delivery work

questionsForInsurer: How will "primarily used" be measured (hours, trips or share of kilometres)?
Will declined applicants be referred to a delivery or commercial product?
whatWouldChangeTheOutcome: Evidence that no suitable delivery coverage exists in the market would raise the accessibility concern.
